newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori rounds on "terrorist" rebels.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori rounds on "terrorist" rebels.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori insisted on Thursday that Peru's hostage crisis was not hurting his country and condemned the Marxist rebels holding 74 hostages in Lima as "terrorists" bent on pointless violence.

The 16-day-old siege at the Japanese ambassador's residence was "an isolated event that is not going to upset the Peruvian economy," Fujimori said in a speech intended to restore confidence in his country's battered reputation.
But he gave no clues about his next move in the crisis.

Speaking at the swearing in of a new Supreme Court president replacing Moises Pantoja, who is one of the captives of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), Fujimori attacked the rebels' claim to be fighting for Peru's poor.

"It is an error to think that the violence that arises from discontent can end poverty," Fujimori said. "Twelve years of violence from Sendero Luminoso (Shining Path guerrillas) and the MRTA -- feverish, destructive violence -- has, on the contrary, made us poorer."
The guerrillas "cannot say that by destroying factories, bridges and by chasing away investors and tourists, poverty is going to be reduced," he added.
Fujimori, whose popularity has been hurt by his country's increasing economic difficulties, said his government would spend 1997 working for "peace and employment."
The guerrillas are still holding 74 hostages and have vowed to use them as bargaining chips for their main demand -- the release of their roughly 400 comrades in Peruvian jails.
"We'll hold them there as long as it takes," MRTA international spokesman Isaac Velazco told Reuters in an interview from Germany.

"The guerrillas can stand it -- they've been trained in the jungle. But can the hostages? If they suffer, the Peruvian government must accept all responsibility for not facilitating a solution to this situation."
Fujimori has flatly rejected the rebel demands.
While Wednesday's release of seven hostages, including four Japanese businessmen, was widely welcomed, it was also seen as helping the rebels' position.
"The situation is becoming more tense as the number of hostages nears a level the guerrillas can control," Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said in Tokyo.
More than 500 people were initially taken hostage at the compound. The women and elderly men were released shortly after and many others were freed over the next two weeks.

The remaining hostages include Fujimori's brother Pedro, two foreign ambassadors, a host of high-ranking government officials and security force top brass, and about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
Continuing their media blitz, the rebels called on world opinion to press for a bloodless end to the standoff, which began on Dec. 17, and challenged Fujimori to make a move.

"We ask the progressive men and women of the world to continue demanding of the Peruvian government a political solution that will bring the freedom of political prisoners and the prisoners of war taken by our commando unit," the MRTA said in a communique sent to Reuters from "somewhere in the central jungle" of Peru before Fujimori's speech.
"It is the Peruvian government's turn to speak," it added.

Fujimori, angered by an impromptu news conference given by the rebels inside the compound on New Year's Eve, has kept his negotiator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, out of the building since Saturday's first meeting with the rebels.

Both sides have waged an intense propaganda battle. The government has cut off the residence's communication links and mostly kept journalists two blocks away from the compound. The MRTA has used methods ranging from cardboard placards to the Internet to get their demands across.
In Ottawa, former hostage Anthony Vincent, Canada's ambassador to Peru, said calm and patience was needed because the guerrillas were prepared to hold out for a long time.

"They obviously have a lot of endurance, they're very well-disciplined, well-organised, very well-armed," he said on a visit to report on the crisis. "I think they're prepared to wait quite a long time if they need to," he told reporters.

While expectations of an early end to the siege have subsided, rumours were still circulating in diplomatic circles of a possible behind-the-scenes deal to fly the rebels to a third country where they would be granted political exile.

Cuba, figuring most prominently in the rumours, reiterated on Thursday a refusal to comment on whether Havana might get involved. Foreign ministry spokesman Miguel Alfonso said he was not aware of a formal request for the government to get involved. And he declined comment when asked if Cuba would be willing to mediate a solution to the crisis if asked, saying the question was too hypothetical.
The MRTA takes its ideological inspiration from Cuba, particularly one of the island's revolutionary heroes, Ernesto "Che" Guevara.
